notes: Original fictional chapter drafted only outside the repository. Four substantive stages near the1500-word centre. No audio, commissioned raster, real-world price or procedure claim.

G14 is restricted to tener que/hay que/ir a + infinitive, deber/necesitar/intentar with known nouns or infinitives, causal por + noun, purpose para + infinitive. No complement que clause, subjunctive, infinitive enclitic, impersonal se or new tense.

English inline meaning captions are permitted by owner RULES; all margin notes remain Spanish. Substantial grammar explanation intentionally exceeds advisory note length to define the forms and translate examples.

The friends agree on their own tasks only. Owner trial acceptance remains15. Luis fixes the shelf foot and receives the fictional two-unit payment; Elena records expense and three remaining. Ceiling/table remain unrepaired. Separate family collection is rescheduled from requested Sunday to Saturdayfive because grandmother leaves Sunday; the transfer has not happened.

Bounded forward G13 recall is consequential, not a recap list: cheap fixed-price foot versus unknown expensive roof work, small shelf worse for Rosa’s large book, actually improved repaired shelf, less cash after payment, happiness at Luis’s work, worse wet-floor zone, equal large boxes requiring a helper, sadness at missing the meeting. No extra scene or three-per-word padding. Redundant unchanged-state assertions were reallocated while retaining all four stages and full practice. Termin a de limpiar was replaced with known termina el trabajo to avoid unintroduced aspectual complementation.

The no-obligation frame now concerns not needing to buy a shelf, while No debemos expresses the safety prohibition; these meanings are not conflated. The forecast uses Después va a tener tres rather than an unclear pre-payment present or an unintroduced después de+infinitive. Actual payment is paga in23, alongside pagar13 and pago24: three meaningful intro uses, no count exception. Para remains within the bounded purpose+infinitive scope.

grammar.title: Gramática
grammar.rule: Tenemos que escribir. Hay que hablar. Vamos a limpiar para proteger los libros.

tables.caption: por · para
rows: por el trabajo de mi casa

grammar.note_en:
An infinitive is the dictionary form of a verb, such as hablar, “speak”, or escribir, “write”. This chapter combines a present verb with an infinitive to express a need, an obligation or a plan. The first verb changes for its subject; the infinitive does not. Tenemos que escribir los nombres y los precios means “We have to write down the names and the prices”. Tengo que ir means “I have to go”; Rosa tiene que devolver el libro means “Rosa has to return the book”. Keep que between tener and the infinitive. Compare No tengo el plan, “I do not have the plan”: without que, tener simply takes the thing possessed. Tienen, “they have”, and tenemos, “we have”, are earlier forms. Tengo, “I have”, is the irregular first-person present; it supplies the first-person obligation tengo que. The reference collects only observed forms. No past tense is introduced.

Hay que + infinitive expresses an impersonal necessity: it does not name a grammatical subject who must do the work. Hay que hablar del techo means “It is necessary to talk about the ceiling” or, in this group discussion, “We need to talk about the ceiling”. Hay stays singular even when several people share the task. This differs from tener que, which makes the responsible person or people explicit. Hay que llevar la cuenta means “The account needs to be taken”; tenemos que dejar abierta la puerta means “We have to leave the door open”. In the latter, abierta agrees with puerta, “door”. No tenemos que comprar otro estante means “We do not have to buy another shelf”; repairing the existing one provides an alternative. It does not mean “we must not”: negating tener que removes the obligation. No debemos dejar los libros debajo del agua means “We must not leave the books beneath the water”, expressing the prohibition directly.

Deber + infinitive also expresses obligation here. Debemos hablar del cuidado de la sala means “We must talk about the care of the room”; debemos guardar el dinero means “We must keep the money”. The chapter uses deber without de. Necesitar means “need”: necesito el precio is “I need the price”; necesitamos dinero para arreglar el techo is “we need money in order to fix the ceiling”. A noun can name the thing needed, and an infinitive can name an action: necesito llevar las dos cajas means “I need to carry the two boxes”. Intentar means “try”: voy a intentar leer el plan means “I am going to try to read the plan”; intento escribir el plan del próximo mes means “I am trying to write the plan for the next month”. These are statements about attempts, not claims that something is already accomplished. An infinitive after another verb keeps its ending: van a arreglar, “they are going to fix”; va a pagar, “she is going to pay”.

Ir a + infinitive expresses a planned or prospective action. Vamos a escribir un plan means “We are going to write a plan”; voy a escribir los nombres means “I am going to write down the names”; ¿Quién va a abrir la sala? means “Who is going to open the room?” The verb after a is the action planned. Contrast the earlier movement construction: voy a la biblioteca means “I am going to the library”, where a leads to a place. Voy a ir recto means “I am going to go straight ahead”: the first voy belongs to the prospective phrase, and the infinitive ir is the intended action. This is not a new future-tense ending. The story also shows mañana van a llevar el plan, “tomorrow they are going to take the plan”. A future time word is compatible with this construction; it does not automatically make every present verb prospective.

Por and para are not freely interchangeable translations of English “for”. This chapter deliberately limits them to two patterns. Por + noun gives a cause or reason: el estante está vacío por la pata débil means “the shelf is empty because of the weak leg”; por la lluvia means “because of the rain”; no puedo venir … por el trabajo de mi casa means “I cannot come … because of the work at my house”. Para + infinitive gives a purpose, the intended result of an action: dejar abierta la puerta para llevar el estante means “leave the door open in order to carry the shelf”; limpio el suelo para proteger los libros means “I clean the floor in order to protect the books”. The cause exists as the reason; the purpose is what someone is trying to achieve. Other uses of either preposition, including exchange, route and duration, are outside this chapter. Por qué, the earlier question “why?”, and porque, the earlier answer “because”, remain distinct spellings and constructions.

The already-taught direct-object words stay before a finite verb: Rosa lo tiene que devolver means “Rosa has to return it”. Lo refers to the borrowed large-print book. The model does not attach the pronoun to an infinitive and introduces no doubled object pronouns or impersonal se. Relative que still links a known thing to an indicative clause: la cuenta que necesitan hoy would be “the account that they need today”; the actual reading gives el precio que necesitan hoy, “the price that they need today”. This is not a new complement clause after a verb of thinking or saying. The question ¿Quién? below techo, “ceiling”, remains a real unanswered question about responsibility.

Próximo means “next”: próximo sábado, “next Saturday”; próximo mes, “next month”. Un mes is “a month”; un año is “a year”. The old notebook account belongs to another year, so it does not supply today’s repair cost. The proposal covers recurring Saturdays in the coming month. Plan is “plan”; reunión, “meeting”; acuerdo, “agreement”; cuidado, “care”; gasto, “expense”; dueño, “owner”. The friends’ agreement allocates their own tasks; it does not grant the owner’s permission or decide the later trial. Arreglar means “fix” here and refers to repairing the foot, the same concrete task described by reparar in chapter13. Limpiar means “clean”; pagar, “pay”. After paying two from five, the room’s small box contains three. The ceiling and the large dismantled table remain unrepaired. The Saturday meeting and the library return have different times: five in the afternoon and nine, earlier in the day. The new family collection time conflicts with Elena’s meeting, so Ana receives the actual proposal and current account. It does not identify the old letter’s sender or the photograph’s child.
